Non-metric Multidimensional Scaling (NMDS)

Source: R/nmds.r
nmds.Rd

Ordinates samples from their distances, for plotting beta diversity, by placing them so that their distances on the plot are in the same rank order as the distances in dm, as nearly as possible. Follows the same procedure as vegan::metaMDS() with its default monoMDS() engine, and gives the same solutions from the same starting configurations, but runs the random starts in parallel C with far less memory.

Usage

nmds(
  dm,
  k = 2L,
  try = 20L,
  trymax = 20L,
  maxit = 200L,
  weakties = TRUE,
  stress = 1L,
  smin = 1e-04,
  sfgrmin = 1e-07,
  sratmax = 0.999999,
  seed = 0L,
  cpus = n_cpus()
)

Arguments

dm

A dist object, such as from beta_div() or bray(), or a symmetric numeric matrix of distances. Must not contain NAs.

k

The number of dimensions. Default: 2

try, trymax

The minimum and maximum number of random starts. Random starts continue past try until the best solution is found again, or trymax is reached. Default: 20 and 20

maxit

The maximum number of iterations for each start. Default: 200

weakties

How to treat tied distances in dm. TRUE, the default, lets them have different distances on the plot (Kruskal's primary approach); FALSE requires their plot distances to be equal too (secondary approach).

stress

Kruskal's stress formula to minimize: 1 (the default) or 2.

smin, sfgrmin, sratmax

Each start stops when its stress falls below smin, when the gradient's scale factor falls below sfgrmin, or when the stress ratio between iterations rises above sratmax (i.e., stress stops improving). Defaults: 1e-4, 1e-7 and 0.999999, as in vegan::monoMDS().

seed

An integer seed for the random starting configurations. The same seed gives the same result. Default: 0

cpus

How many parallel processing threads should be used. The default, n_cpus(), will use all logical CPU cores.

Value

A numeric matrix with one row per sample and one column per dimension, named "NMDS1", "NMDS2", etc., as described in "Ordination result" below. method is "nmds"; eig and prop are NA, as NMDS has no eigenvalues. Then come:

  • stress: The stress of the solution (formula stress), from 0 (perfect) to 1.

  • converged: TRUE if a random start found the best solution again.

  • tries: The number of random starts run.

  • best_try: Which start gave the solution: 0 for the PCoA start, else the random start's number.

Details

Method

NMDS minimizes Kruskal's stress: how far the distances between points \(d_{ij}\) are from the closest sequence \(\hat{d}_{ij}\) that has the same rank order as the distances in dm (found by monotone regression). Formula 1 is \(\sqrt{\sum(d_{ij} - \hat{d}_{ij})^2 / \sum d_{ij}^2}\); formula 2 divides by \(\sum(d_{ij} - \bar{d})^2\) instead.

Each start minimizes stress by steepest descent, with Kruskal's step-size rules, as in Peter Minchin's monoMDS (the default engine of vegan::metaMDS()). This is a line-by-line port of it, so from the same starting configuration, a start gives exactly the same stress and coordinates as vegan::monoMDS().

Steepest descent only finds a local minimum, so, as in metaMDS():

  1. The first start is the PCoA solution, from pcoa().

  2. Then come random starts, with coordinates uniform on [0, 1). A start whose stress is within 0.0005 of the best so far is compared with it by a Procrustes rotation; the best is "found again" when the root mean squared difference is below 0.005 and no point differs by more than 0.01. At least try random starts are run, and more, up to trymax, until the best is found again.

  3. The best solution is centered, rotated to its principal components, and scaled so that its largest distance equals the largest distance in dm. When dm has a maxdist attribute (as from vegan::vegdist()), it is instead scaled to half-change units, as in vegan::postMDS().

Speed and memory

metaMDS() and monoMDS() copy dm into an \(n \times n\) matrix, and keep several arrays with an element for every pair of samples, for every start. nmds() sorts the pairs once, into one shared array of 4 bytes per pair, and each start that runs at the same time needs about 16 more bytes per pair. cpus starts run at once, each on its own thread.

Differences from metaMDS()

  • The random starting configurations come from seed, not from R's random number generator, so set.seed() has no effect, and R's random number stream is left untouched. They differ from the ones metaMDS() draws, so when there are several local minima of similar stress, the two can settle on different ones.

  • The first start comes from pcoa() rather than cmdscale(). The two differ only by rounding (about \(10^{-15}\)), but monoMDS's stopping rule can react to that by stopping an iteration earlier or later, which changes the stress in about the 7th significant digit.

  • Only monoMDS's default "global" model is offered, not its "local", "linear", or "hybrid" ones.

  • metaMDS() given a community matrix, as phyloseq::ordinate() does, first transforms the counts and computes the distances itself. Give nmds() those same distances to get the same solution.

Reproducibility

Results are identical from run to run and for any number of cpus.

Axes are flipped so that each one's coordinate with the largest absolute value is positive.

k larger than \(n - 1\) is reduced to \(n - 1\). A stress below 0.001 gives a warning, as in metaMDS(): there may be too few samples for k dimensions.

Ordination result

Every ordination method (pcoa(), nmds(), and ordination()) returns the same kind of object: a plain numeric matrix with one row per sample (named after the samples) and one column per axis (named "PCoA1", "NMDS1", etc.), so that it can go straight into plot() or a data frame. Its attributes always begin with these three, in this order:

  • method: The method's ID, e.g. "pcoa" or "nmds".

  • eig: Each axis's eigenvalue, or NA for methods without them.

  • prop: The proportion of the total variance that each axis explains, or NA where that isn't defined.

Attributes particular to the method follow them.

References

Kruskal, J. B. (1964). Nonmetric multidimensional scaling: A numerical method. Psychometrika, 29(2), 115-129. doi:10.1007/BF02289694

Minchin, P. R. (1987). An evaluation of the relative robustness of techniques for ecological ordination. Vegetatio, 69, 89-107. doi:10.1007/BF00038690

See also

pcoa(), beta_div()

Examples

    ord <- nmds(bray(ex_counts))
#> Warning: stress is (nearly) zero: there may be too few samples
    ord
#>             NMDS1       NMDS2
#> Saliva -0.3891463 -0.03721917
#> Gums   -0.3951316 -0.05551031
#> Nose    0.3179851  0.53710375
#> Stool   0.4662929 -0.44437427
#> attr(,"method")
#> [1] "nmds"
#> attr(,"eig")
#> [1] NA NA
#> attr(,"prop")
#> [1] NA NA
#> attr(,"stress")
#> [1] 0
#> attr(,"converged")
#> [1] FALSE
#> attr(,"tries")
#> [1] 20
#> attr(,"best_try")
#> [1] 0

    attr(ord, 'stress')
#> [1] 0

    plot(ord, asp = 1)
